groundTruthNarrative: Eastgate's in-house brake bay was closed from 4 Aug to 19 Sep, and the brake services that fell due went to two outside garages. Northfield Motor Services changed the brake fluid on 11 Larkspur vans using a bulk drum that had been open since March and had lost its cap. That fluid had absorbed water, and its boiling point had dropped to about 150°C. On August's flat routes the fault stayed hidden. From 1 September the new Upper Wend routes put long descents into the shared van pool. On those descents the low-boiling fluid vaporised in hot calipers, giving long or soft pedals and fade, including the 9 October near-miss on LK-209. Exactly the 11 drum-fluid vans complained. None of the other vans did: not the two Northfield vans done from a fresh drum, not the 12 Calder Road vans, and not the 13 in-house vans, even though they had the same Tessaro pad batches, the same pooled routes and the same drivers. Two vans re-flushed under warranty on 24 Sep stopped complaining while still running Upper Wend. Northfield warned the workshop coordinator, but he went on leave and nobody acted. Driver technique, the pads and terrain on its own do not explain the complaints. The separate fleet-wide rise in squeal reports is associated with the Tessaro switch, but fresh-pad bedding-in and the FleetCheck rollout confound it. The right move is to pull every Northfield-serviced van now for boiling-point testing and fluid renewal. Disciplining the drivers who complained would punish the people who reported a real defect.

answers.rationale: C6 shows vans are issued from a common pool. The 19 drivers who filed complaints also logged 604 days in non-Northfield vans, 141 of them on Upper Wend, with no brake reports. The same drivers on the same hills produce complaints only in one group of vans, which counts directly against driver technique as the cause. The telematics rise (C1) cannot be broken down by van or driver and does not change this.

C6 shows that the Calder Road and in-house vans carry the same Tessaro batches (T-0612, T-0703), run Upper Wend just as often, and have no complaints. C9 adds that the two Northfield vans with fresh-drum fluid but the same pads did not complain, and that LK-217 and LK-224 stopped complaining after a fluid-only renewal with their pads left in place.

C6 places all 11 complaint vans (E2) in the Northfield group, with exposure, pads and drivers matched against the other vans. C9 identifies the fault introduced there: water-contaminated fluid from an open drum, with boiling points measured near 150°C against 255°C for sealed stock. The initial file alone cannot separate this from the driver, pad and terrain accounts.

The 27 other Eastgate vans ran the same descents (C6: 9–16 Upper Wend days each) and had no complaints, so the terrain does not overheat sound brakes into failure. C9 also shows that the affected vans' brakes were not sound, because their fluid boiling points were far below sealed stock. The terrain only reveals the fluid defect. Manager Rudd's point about timing (E3) and the 'no fault found' inspection (C4, done without a boiling-point tester) are the traps.

E2 notes that FleetCheck went live at all three depots on the same day, yet the other 102 vans produced only 2 soft-pedal reports while Eastgate produced 27. A physical near-miss is documented (E1, C15), and C9 measures degraded fluid. Easier reporting cannot account for a cluster confined to one depot and to specific vans.

The causal case rests on five things. Temporal order: fluid changed in Aug–early Sep, complaints from 2 Sep. Mechanism: low-boiling fluid vaporises on long descents (C9 tests). Covariation: the 11 drum-fluid vans are exactly the 11 complaint vans, while fresh-fluid vans with the same pads and routes have none (C9 with E2 and C6). Main rivals ruled out: drivers, pads and route exposure are matched (C6). Intervention: LK-217 and LK-224 stopped complaining after the fluid-only renewal while still running Upper Wend (C9, E2, C6). C6 alone shows only that the Northfield work, pads and fluid together, is associated with the complaints.

The evidence counts against the link itself. Twenty-seven vans with the same Tessaro batches on the same routes had no complaints (C6, C9), and complaints stopped on two vans whose Tessaro pads were left in place when only the fluid was renewed (C9).

E5 shows co-occurrence: 17 of 21 squeal reports were on Tessaro vans, against a 58% fleet share. But the same note flags that Tessaro vans are the ones with freshly fitted pads, that there is no comparison data for fresh pads of the old brand, and that FleetCheck changed reporting from 1 Aug. Neither read on the optimal path addresses squeal, so causation is not established and nothing counts against the link.

C6 shows the complaining drivers drove other vans on the same descents for 141 days with no complaints, and C9 with C6 shows complaints ended on re-flushed vans under the same pooled drivers. That is evidence against the link itself, not just support for a rival.

Once the fluid is confirmed as the mechanism and the affected group is known, testing and renewing the fluid on every Northfield-serviced van directly removes the hazard. It is cheap, it is quick, and it is validated by the two warranty re-flushes. Nine vans with bad fluid are still running, and there has already been a near-miss. On the initial file alone this action would be premature.

The only explanation still standing is the defective fluid. Under it, warnings punish drivers who correctly reported a real safety defect. E4 and C7 show that the threat is already deterring reports, and the action leaves the faulty vans unaddressed. It does damage under every hypothesis the evidence leaves live.

If the Tessaro pads were shown to cause the squeal, switching back would cut noise reports. That link is only an association, confounded by fresh-pad bedding-in and the FleetCheck rollout (E5). A supplier change at the next cycle does no lasting damage if the link is wrong, but committing to it now is not justified.

Nothing points to bad fluid in the non-Northfield vans: no complaints (C6), and C3 and C14 record sealed bottles. A boiling-point check at the next routine service is a cheap, reasonable precaution, but it is not among the best actions.
With C6 and C9, the mechanism, the exact affected group, the matched rivals and an intervention result are all in hand. That is enough to commit to A1 now, especially with a near-miss on record.

authoringNotes: SEQ design. The initial file names two outside garages but gives no way to tell which vans went where, and it hints that Upper Wend uses 8–9 vans a day. That makes it tempting to read the 11 complaint vans as 'the hill vans'. The natural first read is the maintenance export (C6). It reveals the common pool, the matched pad batches and driver exposure, that all 11 complaint vans are in the Northfield group, and a pointer to Northfield paperwork for a warranty return. Only after C6 can the analyst choose C9 over the parallel-titled Calder Road file (C3). Non-redundancy: C6 alone settles H1, R4 and H2 (driver- and van-level matching), which C9 cannot. C9 alone settles R1 as causal (fluid-specific mechanism, drum-to-van mapping and an intervention), which C6 cannot, because the Northfield vans got pads and fluid together; A1 and SUFF depend on C9 too. C3 and C14 list van IDs with no complaints but give no route or driver exposure, so they do not settle pads or drivers. C4 (no fault found) is a trap countered by its own note that no boiling-point tester was used, and by C9. C1 shows a harsh-braking rise that cannot be attributed to vans or drivers. C2 is an interested vendor. The squeal edge (R3) is association-only from E5 alone and nothing in the catalogue resolves it, which keeps A3 premature. H5 can be dismissed from the initial file, because the app went live at all depots. Hypotheses are worded at the same specificity: no fluid, drum or garage name appears in any hypothesis. Self-check: H4 says 'otherwise in sound condition', so the fact that descents trigger symptoms does not rescue it, and no edge asks whether the terrain is a trigger, to avoid ambiguity between causal and association-only.
